content: The fourth edition of the Guidelines for Drinking-Water Quality, which incorporates the first and second addenda, provides comprehensive recommendations for ensuring safe drinking water. It includes tools such as sanitary inspection packages designed to support small water supplies and offers guidance on surveillance and control of community water systems. These guidelines emphasize the importance of risk-based management, monitoring, and regulation to maintain water quality. The sustainability of rural water service delivery models has been assessed through multi-country reviews, highlighting the need for strong systems and sound investments to accelerate progress in sanitation, drinking water, and hygiene. The 2019 UN-Water Global Analysis and Assessment of Sanitation and Drinking-Water (GLAAS) report underscores the importance of national systems to support drinking water, sanitation, and hygiene, particularly in adapting to a changing world. The World Health Organization (WHO) and other global organizations have developed various resources to address water safety and quality. These include manuals for water safety planning, technical briefs on lead in drinking water, and guidance on managing radioactivity in water. Additionally, tools for selecting water quality field test kits and evaluating household water treatment options have been created to support decision-making and improve water safety. Efforts to professionalize maintenance for rural water services have been documented, with case studies from countries like Kenya demonstrating the social and economic benefits of investing in reliable water infrastructure. Performance-based funding models have also been explored to enhance the reliability of rural water services in Africa. Protecting groundwater and surface water for health is a critical focus, with guidelines available for managing risks in water catchments and ensuring the safety of drinking water sources. The integration of water quality testing into household surveys, as seen in Ecuador, has provided valuable data on microbial safety and seasonal influences on water quality. This approach has highlighted the need for improved risk-based water quality management and the promotion of household water treatment practices. The WHO has also emphasized the importance of equitable water safety planning, climate-resilient strategies, and the use of data to inform decision-making. These efforts aim to strengthen drinking water surveillance, improve data use, and support the implementation of water safety plans at the country level. Case examples from Uganda and Ecuador illustrate how these guidelines and tools have been applied in practice. In Uganda, the government has introduced professionalized maintenance services for rural water supplies, while in Ecuador, water quality testing has been integrated into national household surveys to address data gaps and improve monitoring systems. Overall, these guidelines and resources provide a robust framework for managing drinking water quality, ensuring public health, and achieving sustainable development goals related to water and sanitation.
